title: Approximate thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model in an external magnetic field
abstract: We introduce approximate expressions for the thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model in an external magnetic field. The external field breaks the system's symmetry, which complicates the exact calculation of the free energy. To address this, we write the model in its quaternion representation to apply a small angle approximation with respect to a reference frame. The approximation simplifies the transfer matrix to a centrosymmetric matrix for which the largest eigenvalue is known and depends on the external field strength. We therefore write an approximate expression for the system's free energy and derive the magnetization, susceptibility, internal energy, and specific heat. These results are compared with numerical simulations performed with the BKL algorithm. We find that the approximate expressions and numerical simulations agree in regions where the approximation is valid.
summary: This paper develops approximate analytical expressions for the thermodynamics of the 2D Ising model under an external magnetic field by employing a quaternion representation and small-angle approximation. The derived results for energy, magnetization, and susceptibility are rigorously tested against numerical simulations using the BKL algorithm. It provides valuable insight into how mathematical approximations can successfully model complex physical systems when certain limiting conditions are met.
main_problem: The primary goal is deriving approximate analytical expressions for the thermodynamics of the two-dimensional Ising model when subjected to a non-zero external magnetic field.
main_result: Approximate formulas are derived for key thermodynamic quantities (free energy, magnetization, susceptibility, etc.) which show excellent agreement with numerical simulations in regimes where the small-angle approximation is valid.
method: The method involves reformulating the model using a quaternion representation and applying a small-angle approximation to simplify the transfer matrix diagonalization.
model_or_system: The system studied is the two-dimensional Ising model on a square lattice, described by an Hamiltonian including nearest-neighbor interactions (J) and an external magnetic field (H).
key_observables: Free Energy (F), Magnetization (M), Magnetic Susceptibility ($\chi$), Internal Energy (U), and Specific Heat (C).
important_parameters: The analysis depends on the coupling constant $\phi =  eta J$ and the external field parameter $\psi =  eta H$, with validity requiring both to be small.
main_assumptions: The entire derivation hinges on the application of a small-angle approximation ($\varphi_a \ll 1$), which limits its applicability when $J$ or $H$ are large relative to $T$.
figures_summary: Figures compare calculated thermodynamic quantities ($M, \chi, U, C$) versus varying parameters (like angle $\varphi_a$ or field $H$) for both 1D and 2D systems, validating the approximations against BKL simulation results.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the general framework using quaternion algebra to handle the external field. It then applies the small-angle approximation to simplify the transfer matrix, leading to approximate expressions for all thermodynamic quantities. These analytical results are systematically compared against detailed numerical simulations (BKL algorithm) across various parameter regimes.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the use of quaternion algebra and advanced matrix diagonalization techniques mirrors mathematical tools used in quantum field theory or open quantum systems modeling, making it relevant for theoretical physics practitioners.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Magnetization (M), susceptibility (χ), absolute value of the internal energy (|U|), and specific heat (C) of the two-dimensional Ising model as a function of the angle φa = arctan[sinh(2βH) exp(2βJ)]. Results obtained with the approximate expressions (lines) and nu- merical simulations of lattice sizes N = n×n where n = [20, 50] (symbols) are compared. The cases where J = 0.001 < H = 0.01 (solid lines), J = H = 0.01 (dashed lines), and J = 0.01 > H = 0.001 (dash-dotted lines) are shown. The legends apply to all plots.

FIG. 2. Magnetization (M), susceptibility (χ), internal energy (U), and specific heat (C) of the two-dimensional Ising model shown as a function of the external magnetic field strength H. Results obtained with the approximate expressions (solid, dashed, and dash-dotted lines at T=0.4 (φa ≈0.05), 1 (φa ≈0.02), and 2 (φa ≈0.01), respectively) and numerical simulations of lattice sizes N = n × n where n = [20, 50] (symbols) are compared. The interaction energy is fixed at J = 0.01. The legends apply to all plots.

FIG. 3. Susceptibility (χH=0) of the two-dimensional Ising model with H = 0 as a function of the reduced temperature T/J, where T is the temperature and J is the interaction energy between neighboring spins. Results obtained with the approximate expressions [small angle (dotted lines), mean-field theory (dashed lines), and perturbative expansion (dash-dotted lines)] and numerical simulations of lattice sizes N = n × n where n = [20, 50] (symbols) are shown. The temperature was varied for both values of J (J = 0.01 and J = 1) considered.

FIG. 4. Magnetization (M1D), susceptibility (χ1D), absolute value of the internal energy (|U|1D), and specific heat (C1D) of the one-dimensional Ising model as a function of the angle φa = arctan[sinh(2βH) exp(2βJ)]. Results obtained with the approximate expressions (lines) and numerical simulations of a linear chain of size N = 500 (symbols) are compared. The cases where J = H = 0.01 (dash-dotted lines), and J = 0.01 > H = 0.001 (dashed lines) are shown. The legends shown apply to all plots.

FIG. 5. Magnetization (M1D), susceptibility (χ1D), internal energy (U 1D), and specific heat (C1D) of the one-dimensional Ising model obtained with the exact and approximate expressions (lines) and the numerical simulations of a linear chain of size N = [500, 1000] (symbols) as the external field strength H is varied. The temperature is fixed at T = 1. The legends shown apply to all plots.
